title: Managed Heap, Garbage Collection, and Native Memory

scout.purpose: Master managed heap, garbage collection, and native memory through a production or platform contract supported by causal evidence.
scout.realWorldUse: Android experts need to connect runtime, memory, power, and diagnostic evidence to the actual platform owner and recovery behavior.
scout.outcome: You can design, inspect, test, release, and defend managed heap, garbage collection, and native memory.

blocks.text: ART manages Java and Kotlin objects in a heap with generations or spaces and collector strategies that vary by release. Allocation can be cheap, but allocation rate drives collection frequency and memory footprint. GC begins from roots such as thread stacks, statics, and JNI references, then traces reachability; unreachable objects become reclaimable. Reachable does not mean useful, so a listener, cache, coroutine, or static reference can create a logical leak without a collector defect.

blocks.text: GC work may be concurrent but still requires pauses for roots or phases. Large objects, bitmap pixel storage, direct buffers, graphics allocations, thread stacks, code, mmap files, and native malloc are not explained by Java heap alone. Finalizers and GC requests are not deterministic resource management. Use closeable ownership for files and native handles. JNI local, global, and weak references follow distinct lifetime rules; leaked global references keep managed objects alive.

blocks.text: Correlate heap dumps, allocation recordings, native memory summaries, /proc maps, graphics data, GC events, and process RSS or PSS. A falling Java heap with rising RSS can be expected caching or a native leak. Test repeated journeys to steady state, trim events, backgrounding, large data, rotation, and low-memory devices. Fix ownership and bound caches before tuning collectors. Verify frame, startup, battery, and correctness because reducing allocation by pooling can increase retention or synchronization.

Internals knowledge is useful when it connects a user-visible symptom to the correct owner without turning private implementation into an app dependency. Record the Android build, device, process and compilation state, workload, command or trace configuration, and artifact identity. Combine matching AOSP source with runtime evidence and a controlled intervention. Distinguish managed from native memory, app from system policy, and snapshots from timelines. Test death, pressure, cancellation, idle policy, version differences, and recovery. Preserve the raw evidence and uncertainty. Production applications still use supported APIs; platform changes require security, compatibility, boot, performance, testing, ownership, and rollback evidence.

trap_check.why: It hides an ownership, compatibility, trust, lifecycle, or evidence gap that becomes costly outside the demonstration.
trap_check.fix: Make the disputed boundary explicit and add a representative negative or compatibility test plus operational response.

trap_check.mistake: Treating one successful device, client, model, platform build, or release as proof of the supported contract.
trap_check.why: Advanced Android ecosystems contain version, hardware, consumer, policy, and runtime variation.

recall.prompt: Why can a JNI global reference cause a managed leak?
recall.answer: It is a GC root-like retained reference until explicitly deleted, so the object and its reachable graph remain live.

recall.prompt: What must accompany an expert Android artifact?
recall.answer: Exact source and build identity, supported versions, contracts, tests, measurements, security and privacy review, release evidence, owner, and recovery plan.
They prevent consumers and operators from treating an untested or impossible condition as a silent guarantee.
